     "content": "The episode of the podcast **Denis&Profa** opens in an atmosphere that reflects the seriousness of the topic: an analysis of the derby **Hajduk – Dinamo 2:1**. **Host 1** opens the conversation with the remark that recording outside the European Union was demanding, but that the defeat at Poljud left a deep mark and that this is, as they put it, what interests everyone.\n\nHost 1 announces that they will try not to dwell too long on the introduction and will immediately move on to questions that interest the audience: why the guests were not at Poljud, that is, why they were not in the studio, and whether the defeat can be justified by the circumstances. The conversation is thus set up as a combination of a lighter, relaxed tone and serious football questions.\n\nDuring the introduction, **Host 2** and **Host 1** joke about the current situation and their stay in England, and watching matches in the local atmosphere is also mentioned, which gives the show a recognizable, informal note.",

     "content": "**Host 2** explains that their absence from Poljud was an opportunity which, as he puts it, they welcomed with enthusiasm. It was a meeting with a former Dinamo coach, which the guests described as a rare opportunity that they gladly accepted.\n\nThe guests spent several days in England. Host 2 mentions that they also attended a training session, that yesterday they watched the match between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford, and that they followed the derby in the hotel. In this way, a contrast between English football culture and the Croatian derby is introduced into the conversation.\n\nHost 2 points out that the atmosphere in English football has a special appeal which, as he says, they had been watching in the media since childhood. He emphasizes that this atmosphere is much praised, so his live experience was for him a confirmation of why people love this environment so much. At the same time, he presents the second half of the derby as decisive, with a red card that influenced the course of the match.",

     "subtitle": "Was the defeat justified? Pitch, alibis and the question of a fair picture",
     "screenshot_description": "Split screen with the two hosts discussing alibis; the text “Alibis?” appears on screen as a graphic heading.",
     "content": "Host 1 raises the question of whether the circumstances of the derby, specifically the condition of the pitch and the physical condition of some players, can be taken as an alibi for the defeat. In doing so, he mentions that the players were insufficiently prepared, that is, that they were not at full strength. Host 1 further points out that part of the problem was also that the pitch was poor, so it is possible that Dinamo had to play with one player fewer.\n\n**Host 2** does not accept such an explanation. As he puts it, he would have no alibi because he believes Hajduk was better and deserved to win. He admits that the refereeing and certain situations could have affected the match, but says that this is not the main cause of the defeat.\n\nInstead, Host 2 focuses on Dinamo's play itself, which he describes as poor, while calling the starting lineup problematic. He claims that Dinamo could be compared with Hajduk in terms of individual quality, but that it lagged behind in play, which seems even more disappointing to him.",

     "screenshot_description": "Shot with the two hosts and a graphic showing the team lineup; the names of Hajduk players in the starting line-up are highlighted.",
     "content": "**Host 2** continues with sharp criticism of Dinamo's play. He believes the overall setup of the team was poor and the starting lineup very problematic. As an illustration, he presents an imaginary scenario in which he would write out Hajduk's starting line-up and place it in the Dinamo dressing room, with the message that they were not beaten but were beaten up and outplayed.\n\nHost 2 singles out the play of Hajduk players who, in his assessment, dominated against Dinamo. He ironically comments on the number of successful dribbles and points out that what worries him most is that Dinamo, in his opinion, has better individual players but does not turn them into play.\n\nHe further claims that for a good part of the match Dinamo played in a low or medium block, and that what is expected from a team of its quality did not show. He concludes that this is a worrying pattern, since this was one of the matches in which Dinamo suffered heavy defeats this year.",

     "content": "The conversation then turns to the players' health and the choice of lineup. **Host 2** mentions that one of the key players, Stojković, came to the match after a short period of training, since, according to him, he had only started training on Friday. Host 2 sticks to a statement which, according to his account, coach Kovačević made on Cres, and he considers it unreasonable to expect full form after such a short preparation.\n\n**Host 1** points out that the player had shown himself to be a star on Tuesday, but Host 2 responds that this does not change the situation, because the match had no rhythm. He adds that in that case it would be difficult to bring the player into the game, especially considering the start of the season.\n\nA particular question concerns bringing the player on in the match against Vukovar. Host 1 states that part of the public objected to that move. Host 2 believes that, given the condition of the pitch, it would have been better not to bring him on, but says it is possible that the coach had the idea of bringing rhythm into the game.",

He says that Hapoel was one of the happiest moments of his mandate, alluding to how weak the team was in those matches.\n\n**Host 1** adds that the club openly communicates that the European League is the goal, but that the public considered Dinamo the favorite because of last year's success.      "content": "Host 2 then focuses on the transfer window, which he rates as catastrophically handled. He believes that a person with such decision-making power, along with the resources and contacts that **Zvonimir Boban** has, should not have allowed such a poor transfer window, especially in crucial positions.\n\nAs a specific problem, he cites the signing of players who, in his opinion, did not meet expectations, as well as the absence of reinforcements in some key places, for example in goal. He also criticizes the fact that some young players did not get a chance, which, as he says, is an old topic at the club.\n\nHost 2 links these issues to broader problems in the club. He notes that the public often talks about the stadium and organizational matters, so he believes this situation also affects the atmosphere. He criticizes the way Boban got involved in public debates, rating it as naive in the context of the negative energy that has built up around the coach and the management.",

     "subtitle": "4-3-3 formation without Stojković and Mišić: “Football suicide”",
     "screenshot_description": "Tactical board showing the 4-3-3 formation with empty spots marked for the players who were not on the pitch.",
     "content": "**Host 2** believes that in the derby it was wrong to insist on the 4-3-3 formation without two key players, Stojković and Mišić. He says that such an approach, when main players are missing, is football suicide, because one should adapt to the situation rather than repeat the same pattern as in different circumstances.\n\nHost 2 also criticizes the fact that the team mostly played in the same system, without changes according to the situation. He believes another formation could have been tried and that such a move would have been more logical and desirable than what was seen.\n\n**Host 1** adds that Dinamo mostly played long balls from the back line in attack, while there was no attempt to play through the middle. He believes no attempt was made to compensate for the absence of a playmaker, which in his view was the key failure. Both hosts agree that the problem lies in the organization of the play.",

     "content": "The conversation then turns to the question of the right-back. **Host 1** points out that the coach and the rest of the club get quite angry when that topic is raised, but he emphasizes that, in his opinion, Kovačević is not the biggest problem. He believes the solutions in that position were inconsistent and that the coach shifted part of the problem onto the players.\n\n**Host 2** believes that Tadinac's quality does not meet Dinamo's demands, especially in big matches, where the team defends in a low block. He says the player has explosiveness and sometimes a good cross, but that he is not a young player nor does he have great selling potential.\n\nHost 2 especially singles out Galešić as a player who consistently showed quality and deserved a chance at right-back, but remained outside the first team. He adds that if the club has no homegrown right-back, it should review how the academy functions, since otherwise a long-term gap would be created.",

He believes the preparation was insufficiently good and that the coaching approaches were too general for a match that required a high level of concentration.\n\nHost 2 states that it is not hard to prepare for Dinamo, because all coaches know how that team plays, but that this was still not exploited. He stresses that Dinamo's style of play and patterns are already known, so the question is why there was no clearer plan for Hajduk.\n\nAs an example, he mentions that some claimed the rain was the main reason for the poor play, while, in his opinion, Hajduk was better precisely when the conditions were irregular. Host 1 agrees that such situations also affected the psychological element of the match.",

     "subtitle": "Kovačević's coaching career: has he proven that he is right for Dinamo?",
     "screenshot_description": "Shot of the two hosts with a graphic showing an overview of coaching careers; the caption “Is he right for Dinamo?” appears on screen.",
     "content": "The conversation then turns to **Kovačević's** coaching career. **Host 1** concludes that he has met his goals, but emphasizes the difference between the question of whether someone is a good coach and the question of whether they are the right one for a particular club. He points out that the long-term leadership of Dinamo is especially demanding and that short-term results are not always the only indicator.\n\n**Host 2** cites examples from European football, such as Guardiola and Klopp, to show that even successful coaches sometimes find themselves in a situation where a process comes to an end. He believes a coach can be good, but that the energy in the team sometimes gets lost, so the relationship has to be rebuilt.\n\nHost 2 especially emphasizes that Kovačević never got enough time and complete freedom in building the squad at Dinamo. He recalls that before that he worked at Belupo, where he often changed formations, which, in his view, shows his ability to adapt.",

     "content": "**Host 1** states that after the match Kovačević made a statement about the substitutions, in which he said that the changes had been prepared but came too late. He believes such an explanation left an impression of incompleteness and that it is not clear whether it was a failure in managing the match or due to other factors.\n\n**Host 2** believes the substitutions were not the main problem. In his view, if the changes had come a few minutes earlier, it probably would not have significantly changed the outcome. He sees the problem in the preparation of the match and in the starting line-up, not in how the players were substituted during the game.\n\nIn this part, the conversation closes with a brief contradiction between the two hosts about how relevant the coach's statements were. The final part of the segment marks the transition to closing remarks and an announcement of the continuation of the conversation about the match.",

   "sections": [
    {
     "subtitle": "Refereeing at the derby: the referee as a goat horn where nobody looks for a culprit",
     "screenshot_description": "Two hosts in the studio for the podcast Podcast 8_24 discussing the referee's decisions from the derby; the episode title “Hajduk - Dinamo 2:1 / Denis&Profa” is on screen.",
     "content": "The conversation about the derby moves on to refereeing, and **Host 2** immediately points out that one should not dwell too much on the referee's decisions. In his opinion, the refereeing in that match was what it was, and the referee Pajač, as he says, “was Pajač”. He adds that, had the outcome been the opposite, Hajduk would be “spitting fire” over the yellow cards and decisions that went in Dinamo's favor, which shows how much the result shapes the perception of individual situations.\n\n**Host 1** agrees that the referee's decisions are part of the story, but holds that they are not the reason for the defeat. As an argument, he cites that everyone is involved in the debate about refereeing, including fans on social media, who shifted the focus to the referees instead of their own team's play. He stresses that he finds it funny that, alongside the eternal complaints about “who is the bigger crook”, people forget that the derby with Hajduk does have its statistics. According to him, there were eight derbies in total under this referee, and Hajduk won five and drew three of them, which, as he himself stresses, is an accurate figure “if I am not mistaken”.\n\nThe discussion shows two currents of thought: one, represented by Host 2, calls for an objective analysis without excuses, while the other, represented by Host 1, warns about hypocrisy in the public debate about referees.",

     "subtitle": "Yellow and red cards: when things are compared against standards",
     "screenshot_description": "Footage from the derby showing a foul and the referee's reaction; a marker for the cards or a side-by-side comparison of situations is on screen.",
     "content": "The hosts go on to discuss the cards. **Host 2** criticizes the way the referee explains his decisions during the match and the podcast, stating that referees should only give the foul and show the card, without constantly explaining. For the situation that preceded the red card, he says that, based on what he saw on his phone without additional camera angles, such an offence deserves a red card, while it later turned out that the player was not punished in that way.\n\n**Host 1** adds that the situation was even more careless given the condition of the pitch, which was slippery and difficult to play on. Although he does not justify the refereeing, he says it is funny to him when someone claims that the player should have received two yellow cards, because, as he explains, rules do not work that way when it comes to multiple offences by one player. He recalls that when the player came onto the pitch he immediately thought a red card would follow, because the player kicked the ball away with his foot and then reacted very impulsively.\n\nThe conclusion of the discussion is that the cards were controversial, but that no single referee could be the only reason for the outcome. The hosts agree that this is not an excuse for Dinamo's play, but that consistency in interpreting the rules is needed.",

     "subtitle": "From the National Football Museum to Old Trafford: an anecdote about Ronaldo and Kranjčar",
     "screenshot_description": "Photograph from Old Trafford or from the National Football Museum showing a wall and a figure of Cristiano Ronaldo; the host holds a phone with a photograph.",
     "content": "The conversation turns to a personal anecdote. **Host 1** says that on that day they visited the National Football Museum, where he was surprised by the large presence of Cristiano Ronaldo. After that they arrived at Old Trafford, and the first photograph he took was the one with two of his “biggest favourites”: Ronaldo's goal against Portsmouth, known as the “famous rocket”, and Niko Kranjčar in the wall. As he points out, the ball went past Kranjčar at that moment, which was especially interesting to him.\n\nAccording to his account, after he saw the exhibition, he was also disappointed: when he asked about something he had been looking for, he did not get an answer, so, as he puts it, he “attacked the man”, only to be told that everything was sold out. In the end, he still managed to get a greeting for one of the fan groups.\n\n**Host 2** remarks that such stories can easily be used for jokes, so the conversation becomes a relaxed anecdote, without deeper political or football significance, but with a clear sense of the atmosphere of English football.",

     "subtitle": "The main reason for Dinamo's decline: a question without a simple answer",

     "content": "The hosts raise the question that they consider key: what is the main reason why Dinamo is playing worse than last season. **Host 1** presents the audience's question and asks for it to be explained “honestly”, and **Host 2** replies that the answer lies in a combination of several factors, but that it is primarily visible in the organization of the club and the squad.\n\n**Guest 2** points out that pressure on the coach and the team is decisive. He believes the coach is under strong pressure and that this is reflected in the players, who, as he says, are “shaken”. He adds that the negative energy from the top of the club has spilled over to the coach and players, which resulted in uncertainty on the pitch.\n\nHost 1 finally returns to the shared conclusion: first of all, one needs to look at how the club approached the transfer window, which will be the topic in the next few minutes of the conversation.",
